1-2: Adding in a clever order: numbers paired to make ten or a round number first.
A hidden number with a step or two done to it: undo the steps, the last one first.
Adding the same number again and again: counting the groups.
Adding nines as tens and taking the ones back.
A run of numbers added by pairing the first with the last.
Taking away by counting up from the smaller number.
A long row of plus and minus signs, taken in pairs that each give the same.
Taking away many numbers one after another: add them up first, then take the sum away.
Multiplying in a clever order: a two and a five first, to make ten.
The same number added and then taken away again cancels out, whatever lies between.
A sum already known, with one of its numbers then made bigger or smaller: the new total comes from the old one, with no adding again.
Two subtractions with the same answer: both numbers made bigger or smaller by the same amount.
Two totals compared without working either out: their numbers matched one with another, or the part both share set aside.
Two children with different numbers of things: to have the same, the one with more gives the other half of the difference.
Missing digits in an addition written in a column: the ones first, then the tens with what was carried.
Digit cards made into numbers with the biggest or the smallest sum: the big digits go into the tens.
One number crossed out of a list so that the others add up to a given total: it is what the whole sum is over by.
A little table whose rows and columns are added up: all the rows together make as much as all the columns.
A whole that is a few things and half of itself more, such as a catch of fish: the few are the other half.
A snail that climbs so far by day and slips back less by night: on its last day it reaches the top and does not slip.
3-4: Heads and legs of two kinds of animals: suppose all were of one kind, and each animal of the other kind adds the difference in legs.
A hidden number found from two ways of working on it that give the same result, such as adding 12 and tripling it.
Two purchases, or a full and a half-full can, that differ in one part: the difference of the totals is that part's price or weight.
Numbers in a row or round a circle where any three neighbours add up to the same: the numbers repeat every three places.
Two numbers from their sum and their difference: take the difference away, then halve what is left.
A common factor taken out: 17 × 4 + 17 × 6 worked out as 17 × 10.
Multiplying by 9 or 11 as by 10, with a small change.
Plus signs put between some of the digits 1 to 9, the others joined into bigger numbers, so that the total is a given number.
Something that doubles every day and is full on a given day: one day earlier it was half full.
Doubling and halving: one factor doubled and the other halved.
The last digit of a sum or a product, found from the last digits alone.
Two numbers from their sum and their product: the pairs of numbers that multiply to the product, tried in turn.
Brackets put into a row of numbers and signs: where they go changes the result, and one place gives the biggest.
Shots at a fair, a few to begin with and more for every hit: the shots taken are the first ones and those earned.
The totals of every two of three numbers: all three together are half the sum of those totals.
An addition worked back from how much the sum is more than each of its two numbers: each of those is the other number.
Strengths or prices tied together in a chain, each so many times another: all counted in units of the smallest.
Leftovers made into new pieces: every few used pieces give one more, which is used in its turn.
An answer chosen by estimating: each number rounded, and only one of the options is near.
Nine dates in a square on a calendar page: they add up to nine times the one in the middle.
5-6: Sums of 1, 11, 111 and so on, column by column.
A chain of operations on a hidden number, undone from the end.
Products grouped into tens, hundreds and thousands.
A number trick that gives the same answer whatever the number thought of.
A number from a total of parts of it: the number and half of it, or a half and a third of it, make a given sum.
A two-digit number and the number with its digits swapped.
The sum of all the digits of all the numbers in a range.
A difference of two squares, as a sum times a difference.
A sum written in letters, each letter a digit and no two letters the same: the digits that make it true.
A long sum of alternating plus and minus signs, taken in pairs.
A block of digits written twice, such as abcabc: the number is the block times 1001, and longer repeats work the same way.
Digits taken off the end of a number, or written on at its ends: the change is the place value of what moved.
A four-digit number aabb that is a square: it divides by 11, so its square root does too.
Digits placed into a product to make it as big as it can be: the biggest digit goes where it is multiplied most.
Groups of two sizes in equal numbers, such as families with one cat and families with five: together they count as the size in the middle.
Bounds from the number of digits: which numbers stay two-digit or three-digit when they are multiplied.
Amounts that become equal once each has its own step done to it, one more, one less, doubled or halved: all written through that equal result.
A number that is a given number of times the sum of its digits: its digits found from what each place is worth.
A round number less a little, such as a thousand less seven: its digits are nines and what is left over.
Different whole numbers with a given average: one of them is as big as it can be when the others are the smallest.
